gates.why: Requirement 1, and the rung the rest of the milestone stands on. `go 1.22` is the directive that changes the meaning of code already in the tree rather than merely permitting new code: a variable declared by a `range` or a three-clause `for` is per-iteration from this rung on, and every closure in this repository that captured one means something different after this line is edited than before it. It is also the rung `log/slog` needs for its `vet` analyser and the rung `math/rand/v2` needs to exist at all. Exact rather than a minimum, for the reason the gate documents: a module that declares a later version has taken the whole ladder in one line while the constructs it enables are still absent from the tree. Worth 2 of 31 because it is one line, and because a tree that edits only this line has changed the semantics of the four sites the two counts below name -- two copy workarounds and two reads past a parameter -- and fixed none of them.

Requirement 2's first half, counted. Before the rung requirement 1 raises, the only way to give a goroutine its own copy of a loop variable was to pass it as an argument to a function literal that shadows the name, and this tree does it twice: `go func(srv *HTTPServer) { ... }(srv)` in `api/server/server.go` and `go func(tid int) { ... }(tid)` in `api/server/services/services_task.go`. At the new rung both are ceremony around a variable that is already per-iteration, and requirement 2 asks for both the parameter and the argument to go. The census counts a function literal declared inside a loop that either takes a parameter named after one of the loop's variables or is invoked with one of them, which is exactly and only that shape: two on the tree this step starts from, zero when the clause is done. Either half alone is enough to be counted, and that is deliberate: the first version of this census read parameter names only, and a tree that kept both workarounds and renamed their parameters read zero -- 2 of this family for a rename. The argument is written at the call site in the loop's own words and a rename cannot move it. Graded, so removing one of the two earns half. It is worth 2 rather than 1 because it is the only gate in this family that reads the *clean-up* half of requirement 2 -- the half that changes no behaviour and is therefore invisible to every other check in the package.

Requirement 2's second half, and the defect it exists for. A typed pass over the module reports a reference to a range or three-clause loop variable from inside a function literal that declares a parameter of that variable's own type: a closure handed the value it is supposed to work on that reaches past the parameter for the loop's variable anyway. Two on the tree this step starts from and both are in one function: `volumeDetachAll` in `api/server/router/volume/volume_routes.go` ranges a channel into `service`, builds a closure that already receives the service it is supposed to work on as `svc`, and then reaches past it for the outer `service` twice -- once to name an error and once to key the reply map -- before enqueuing the whole thing to run later on another goroutine. That is a live aliasing bug at the old rung, and requirement 1's directive does not fix it: a per-iteration `service` is still the wrong variable for a closure that was handed `svc`. It has to be read and corrected. Two references, so the gate moves a reference at a time. The sibling handler thirty lines above has the same shape and uses only `svc`, which is what makes this one legible as a bug rather than a style. Decided by type rather than by name, and the first version of this gate was an AST census that decided it by name -- every identifier naming a loop variable, inside any literal that had any parameter of its own. That reading is wider than requirement 2 states and it fails an honest tree. Requirement 4 invites a registration loop, and a solver who writes the dispatch inline -- `m.HandleFunc(p.method+" "+p.path, func(w http.ResponseWriter, req *http.Request) { ... })`, reading the loop's pattern from inside the handler -- has written the correct thing at this rung: nothing handed that literal the pattern, and the variable it reads is per-iteration. Measured, a reference tree rewritten that way read 2 under the census -- the baseline, no credit at all, for a tree with the bug fixed -- and reads 0 here, because `w` and `req` are not a `types.StorageService` and nothing was handed a copy. A copy the loop body makes of its own variable is followed, though: `s := service` written inside the loop and then read from inside the literal that was handed the service is this same defect one binding further out -- the parameter is still unused, and the copy is the workaround the count beside this gate retires -- so it is reported, and so is a copy of that copy. Only a short declaration whose whole right-hand side is the variable counts; a value computed from it is a different value. Measured: 2 findings on the tree this step starts from and 0 on the reference solution with the rule as without it, and on a constructed tree holding all of these shapes at once the copy and the copy of the copy are reported while the parameter-using literal, a value derived from the loop variable and a `ServeMux` handler are not. The pass type-checks the module to answer that, so a tree it cannot type-check scores zero rather than reporting an empty population: the last capture cannot be retired by breaking the build. Worth 4, twice the clean-up half beside it, because the corpus prices the outcome of this and not the reading: the recorded answer for a bulk detach is the same either way on a single-service configuration, which is the only configuration the corpus has. Nothing outside this gate reads the defect at all. 4 is also the ceiling: it is the price of retiring the logging library from all nineteen packages, and two references cannot be worth more than that. What 4 buys is the order of the two ways to finish this step badly. Measured at 2 and then at 3, a tree that leaves both halves of requirement 2 undone scored ABOVE a tree that renders every log line in this repository in a different dialect of logfmt -- and the migration line leads with the loop variables. At 4 against the rendered form's 4, requirement 2 as a whole is 6 of this family and the form is 4, so skipping the clause the line names first costs more than getting the form wrong, while inside requirement 2 the ceremony stays cheaper than the defect.

Requirement 3's endpoint, and the largest single weight in this family. Eighteen packages reach the library through the import graph this gate reads, which is the baseline beside it; a nineteenth, `drivers/storage/mock`, reaches it behind a `mock` build constraint no default build satisfies, and the census below is what covers that one. Thirty files import the library in all. Strict rather than graded, for the reason the previous two milestones made their library gates strict: the cheapest tree that satisfies a proportional reading is the one requirement 3 rules out by name. Give the library a first-party name -- one `api/types/logging` package that re-exports `Fields`, `Entry` and `ParseLevel` -- point the other thirty files at that, and eighteen of the nineteen importers are gone for a rename that has retired nothing. The gradient that reading deserves is the census beside this gate, which moves a file at a time and is why this one can state the endpoint. Note what it does not ask: the library stays in `go.mod` as an indirect requirement after the last first-party import of it is gone, because `github.com/akutz/gofig`, `github.com/akutz/golf` and `github.com/akutz/goof` all reach it, and this gate reads the repository's own packages rather than the requirement list.

Requirement 3, counted over the source rather than over the build, and the finer of the two gradients: thirty files import the library. The census is syntactic and filesystem-scoped, so `drivers/storage/mock/mock_driver.go` -- which carries a `mock` build constraint no default build satisfies, and is the one file of the thirty in that position -- is counted here and is invisible to the import graph above, which is why that gate reads eighteen packages where the tree holds nineteen. A tree that leaves that file is not done, and this is the only gate that says so. Thirty-one files name the library and thirty import it: `api/server/handlers/handlers_schema_validator.go` carries the import commented out, which the census does not count and neither does this baseline.

Requirement 3's complement, and the gate that separates the migration from the deletion. Absence of the old library is satisfied by a tree that stopped logging, and the corpus would barely notice: of the roughly eleven hundred recorded exchanges, six lines in two expect files hold a rendered log line. Five packages is a floor rather than a target -- nineteen hold a file that imports the library today and how many of them need the new one is a question about how the port is factored, not about whether it was done. A tree that funnels every call through one first-party package would read 1 here and is the tree the strict gate above already rules out; five is the number below which no honest factoring of this port can land.

Requirement 3's second library. `api/server/server.go` translates the logger's level into the facade's level with a seven-arm switch and installs an appender that writes the facade's records through the logger. It is the only package in the repository that touches it, nothing else in the repository logs through it, and with the library beneath it retired there is nothing left for the translation to translate. Strict, but worth 1: it is one import in one file, and the seven-arm switch beneath it is priced by `build-all` and by the corpus rather than by a weight here.

The bridge between the two libraries requirement 3 retires, and a separate gate from the one above because it is a separate import path and the gate matches the path exactly rather than by prefix. This is the one an otherwise complete port is most likely to leave behind: it is imported under an alias, `glogrus`, so a candidate grepping for the retired library's name does not find it.

Requirement 4's endpoint. One package imports the router -- `api/server/server_http.go` -- and it uses three names from it: `mux.NewRouter` to build the table, `mux.Router` as the type it returns, and `mux.Vars` to read the path variables back out of the request inside every handler. Strict, though at a baseline of one strict and graded are the same number; it is written strict to say which of the two readings is meant. Worth 2 because it is the endpoint of a clause whose whole difficulty is elsewhere: the routing probe in the regression family is what prices doing it faithfully, and this gate prices doing it at all.

Requirement 4's other half, and the one a candidate who ports only the router will miss. `api/context/context.go` imports the second gorilla package to clear the per-request value map the first one populates; it is the only reason this repository has ever imported it, and the two are retired together or not at all. A tree that keeps it is carrying a dependency whose only caller is gone, and -- worse -- is still calling into a global map that nothing writes to any more.

Requirement 4's complement, counted as adoption because there is nothing to retire on this side. The standard router grew wildcard patterns and an accessor for them in Go 1.22, and the accessor is a method on the request rather than a package-level function, so there is no import to check and no package-qualified selector to count: the census counts calls to a `PathValue` method on anything, which is zero on the tree this step starts from. A floor of one rather than a target, because how many call sites a faithful port needs is a question about how the handler reads its variables and not about whether the clause was done. It is worth 1 of 31 because a port that reads the variables some other honest way -- matching the pattern itself, carrying its own table -- has not made a mistake; it has not used the thing requirement 4 names, and that is worth a gate and not a family.

Requirement 5's endpoint. One package imports it: `api/server` seeds a generator from the clock and draws three numbers from it to name a server. Worth 1 because that is the whole of the clause and it is eight lines. What makes it more than a rename is that the replacement package is not a superset: there is no `NewSource`, no `Intn` and no `Read`, so the constructor has to become `rand.NewPCG` or the top-level generator, and the three draws have to become `IntN`. `build-all` hears a candidate who tries the rename.

Requirement 5's complement. One package, because one package is all there is. Both halves are here for the reason every absent/present pair on this ladder is: absence alone is satisfied by a tree that deleted the randomisation and named every server the same thing, which the corpus would not notice -- the recorded expectations normalise the server name away, because it was random when they were recorded.

Requirement 3's rendered form, and the only gate in this family that reads what the port does rather than which import paths it names. It exists because the price was measured and the price was wrong. Twelve call sites in this repository log without a context -- six that write a line through the library's package-level logger, two that take its `io.Writer` to dump an HTTP request into, two that reach into it for the formatter and hooks a fresh context inherits, and two that set its level from configuration and from the command line -- and their lines land on the same standard error as every other one. The rest of this family would score a port that renders every one of them in a different dialect of logfmt at 1.0: a tree built to do exactly that, by handing the repository's handler through to `slog.NewTextHandler`, took the whole migrated family, failed three of the nine tests `probe:logging` then graded -- four of the thirteen it grades now -- and lost three of the corpus's 1 118 inputs, for a measured 0.991141 overall. That is 0.009 of reward for a change to every log line in the repository, and requirement 3's longest block is the one describing that line. The two tests are in this family and not that one because they are the only two in the directory that fail on the tree this step starts from, and they fail there for a reason that is about the milestone rather than the form: that tree has no `log/slog` in it, so the standard library's own logger is still its own out-of-the-box default and renders `2009/11/10 23:00:00 INFO msg key=value`. They name no first-party identifier -- they ask `slog.Default()` for a line and read the bytes -- so they pin the requirement rather than the reference solution's spelling: any tree whose logging goes through the standard library at all has a `slog.Default()`, and the requirement is about what it writes. Worth 4 of 31: an eighth of this family, and the largest single weight in it that is not an import path. 5 was measured first, and it moved the `NewTextHandler` tree from 0.991141 to 0.900204 -- the price of the rendered form from 0.009 of reward to 0.09. It came back to 4 to leave requirement 2's two clauses, 6 together, above this one, which is the order the migration line states; at 4 the same tree is 0.9196 and the form still costs eight times what it cost before this gate existed. Either way the untouched step-4 tree is where the arithmetic in NOTES 4.5.2 puts it, because this gate reads 0 there too.

cancellation.why: Five tests, 3.0 s together on the finished tree and 3.0 s on the tree this step starts from; the two controls account for nearly all of it, one of them deliberately waiting two seconds for a slow answer. Every failure path in the package is a bounded select, so the budget is there for a tree that will not start a server at all rather than for one that merely fails.

deadlines.why: Four tests, and each of the two graded ones now drives its key at two values in turn rather than at one, so the package starts six servers instead of four: 56.4 s together on the finished tree and 41.2 s on the tree this step starts from, where the two graded tests fail early. Neither is the number the budget has to clear. A tree that adds a draining stop and keeps the 2017 substring sniff deadlocks every close, and this package's teardown gives up on a stop after 30 s rather than joining the deadlock -- six servers, so three minutes of teardown on top of the waiting the tests do anyway: measured at 236.6 s on that tree, with all four assertions still reported correctly. The budget is set above that so a deadlock elsewhere in the tree costs this package time and not its answers.

errstatus.why: Six tests sharing one server, 1.07 s together on the finished tree and 1.07 s on the tree this step starts from, where the three graded tests fail on the first response they read. Neither is the number the budget has to clear. Every way this package can wait is bounded by the package itself: sixty seconds for a server that never finishes starting, fifteen for a request that is never answered, thirty for a stop that never returns. Twenty-one requests are issued in all, so the arithmetic worst case -- a server that answers every one of them just too slowly to count -- is 315 s of requests on top of a minute of start and half a minute of stop, and the budget sits above that. Bounding rather than waiting is deliberate: a tree whose server has been broken elsewhere should fail these assertions and say so, not take the package's other answers down with it.

errwrap.why: Six tests that construct errors and ask questions of them in process -- no server, no listener, no clock. 0.005 s together on the finished tree and 0.006 s on the tree this step starts from. The budget is two minutes because the only way this package can be slow is a tree that takes a long time to compile, and a compile is the one thing a test timeout should never be the first to notice.

logging.why: Eighteen tests that build a context and log to it in process -- no server, no listener, no clock -- thirteen graded bounds, the two that read the logger no context configured, and three controls that ask the same of the harness itself. 0.02 s together on the tree this step starts from: every one of them writes a handful of lines and reads them back. Two minutes for the reason the other the compile, not the tests. The one thing this package does that is not ordinary is redirect file descriptors 1 and 2 into a pipe for the duration of each call and restore them afterwards, including on the way out of a panic; the reader is drained in a goroutine so a logger that writes more than a pipe buffer cannot block, and the first of the three controls is there to fail loudly if any of that stops working.

routing.why: Eight tests against one server. The package starts a single real server on a loopback port with a single vfs service in TestMain, seeds one volume through it, and every test drives raw requests at that one instance: 34 request/response pairs in all, 1.08 s together on the tree this step starts from, because the requests are loopback round trips against an in-process driver. The budget is ten minutes rather than one for the failure modes, not for the passing case. A routing table the candidate has changed fails in two shapes. The fast shape is a pattern the standard router rejects: `net/http.ServeMux.Handle` panics rather than returning an error, the panic happens in TestMain before the first test, and the binary dies in 0.099 s reporting nothing -- measured, with a deliberately malformed pattern -- which is 0/8 and costs no clock at all. The slow shape is a server that starts and then answers late or not at all, and that one is bounded by the deadlines the package carries rather than by the harness killing it: 20 s to start, 10 s to become ready, 15 s on each of the seed request and the 34 graded ones, 10 s to stop, which is 550 s if every single request runs out its deadline. Ten minutes sits above that, so `go test -timeout` never truncates the run and every assertion is reported as its own pass or fail; the 660 s hard timeout sits above the `go test` one so that the Go-side timeout is always what fires, since that prints a panic dump after the `--- PASS` lines the parser has already seen, while a hard kill would lose them. Retry, added in migration review round 1 (2026-10-04): this package's subject carries the race steps 06-08 already retry for -- `taskTrack` in `api/server/services/services_task.go` takes the next task id from `len(s.tasks)` under the read lock and inserts under the write lock, so two overlapping registrations can claim one id and a request can wait on a task nobody completes. It is verbatim in the 2017 tree and no step touches it. Step 05 had been left without the retry as a known-open; the round-1 oracle gate then lost `TestTheOrdinaryRoutesStillAnswer` on the reference tree (probe:routing-controls, 0.994030), and the same collected tree reproduced it once in six runs by hand: `GET /snapshots` waited out its 15 s deadline, the other five runs passed in 1.07 s. `lib/gates.py` here carries step 06's `probe_run`/`probe_once` verbatim so the flag is read. A tree that is broken fails both executions and is still failed.

schema.why: Five tests. Three of them walk the whole repository: one parses every `.go` file in it, one finds every schema document in it and asks `go/build` for the embed patterns of the directories above each one, from the document's own directory up to the repository root, and the third reads the fourteen makefiles it passes on the way. The other two parse the schema document and drive the validator. 0.103 s together on the tree this step starts from and 0.096 s on the finished one, measured five tests at a time. Seven hundredths of that is the literal walk, which is the only one that parses every `.go` file in the repository; the embed reader asks `go/build` rather than the parser and the other three are a hundredth of a second each. The budget is two minutes because the only way this package can be slow is a tree that takes a long time to compile, and a compile is the one thing a test timeout should never be the first to notice.

shutdown.why: Four tests, 40.6 s together on the finished tree and 4.2 s on the tree this step starts from, where every stop returns at once and every assertion fails the moment it is made. Neither is the number the budget has to clear. The worst measured case is the half-done tree that adds a draining stop and keeps the 2017 substring match, which deadlocks the close: there each test waits out its own ceiling and then pays a further 30 s of bounded teardown for a stop that was never going to return, 288.4 s in all, with all four failures still reported rather than lost with a killed binary. A tree that drains but sets no deadline is the other slow case, at 80.7 s. The budget sits well above the deadlocking tree because bounding the teardown exists precisely so that this package still answers on a tree whose close hangs, and a package timeout would take those answers away again.

store.why: Ten tests that construct a `types.Store` and read values back out of it in process -- no server, no listener, no clock. 0.014 s together on the tree this step starts from. Two minutes for the same reason as the package above: the compile, not the tests.

surface.why: Two tests, each of which starts an embedded server and a client through `libstorage.New` and makes one request: 2.3 s together on the finished tree and 2.2 s on the tree this step starts from. The budget is sized for the two ways a tree can be slow here rather than wrong -- `libstorage.New` itself hanging, which the helper gives up on after 60 s, and a stop that never returns, which the teardown gives up on after 30 s. Measured against the deadlocking tree: 62.4 s, both assertions still reported.

regression.why: Requirement 8. Inherited and still a bound rather than a milestone, and in this milestone it is the check most likely to be the first to speak. Three of the five clauses are the kind of port where the obvious edit does not compile: `math/rand/v2` has no `NewSource`, no `Intn` and no `Read`, so `rand.New(rand.NewSource(time.Now().UnixNano()))` and the three `Intn` calls beneath it all have to be rewritten rather than re-imported; the standard router panics at registration time on a pattern it cannot parse, which is a run-time failure rather than a compile-time one and is the reason the routing probe exists as well as this gate; and `log/slog` has no `Entry` type, so every one of the thirty files that names one has to be rewritten rather than re-imported.

Requirement 8. Computed from the import graph, so a dependency copied back into the repository under any directory name and rewired with a replace directive is still third-party source here. The same requirement has a second reading, because the graph cannot see a dependency whose source has been copied *into* the main module and given a first-party import path: every first-party file is also hashed, whitespace removed, against every .go file in the module cache the image ships, and a file that matches one of them is that dependency's source under another name. This milestone retires four third-party libraries at once. Copying any of the four in under a first-party name -- a `api/types/logrus` holding the text formatter, an `api/server/mux` holding the router -- is the shape the cheapest wrong answer takes, and it is the shape this gate is looking for.

Requirement 8. `replace` would let a package be aliased back in under a name of the candidate's choosing; `ignore` would let a file that no longer compiles disappear from every `./...` pattern, including the import graph the gates above read. Note what this does *not* forbid: three of the libraries this milestone retires are reached by dependencies of this module as well as by this module, so they stay in `go.mod` as indirect requirements after the last first-party import of them is gone. The gates that read this milestone read the import graph, not the requirement list, for exactly that reason.

Requirement 8. The tree this step starts from is `gofmt -s` clean -- 0 dirty files out of 163 -- so the baseline is zero and any excursion is new. The standard router's patterns are string literals and cost this gate nothing; what does is the shape of the work, which is thirty files edited by hand in one pass, and the commonest way that ends is one import block left in the order the editor found it.

Requirement 8, same shape: the tree this step starts from leaves `go vet ./...` silent, so the bound is silence. `vet` earns its place here rather than merely keeping it, because at the rung requirement 1 asks for it runs the `slog` analyser: a structured call whose arguments do not pair up into keys and values -- the single commonest mistake in a hand port off a `WithFields` map -- is reported by name, and this is the gate that hears it. It is also the tool that notices a `printf` verb that no longer matches what it is handed, which is how a message assembled out of a retired `Entry` goes wrong.

Requirement 8's last clause. The check class is SA1019, deprecated identifiers, and the baseline is zero. Requirement 5 is the clause that puts it under load: `math/rand`'s top-level `Seed` has been deprecated since Go 1.20 and the package's own documentation has pointed at `math/rand/v2` since Go 1.22, which is the rung requirement 1 asks for. A tree that raises the directive and leaves the generator where it is is not a partial answer to two requirements; it is a tree that scores the rung and loses this bound.
Requirement 6: silencing a tool is not fixing what it found. Zero today, and the bound is zero. `//lint:ignore SA1019` over an `io/ioutil` import is the specific thing this forecloses.
Requirement 6. One `t.Skip` exists in the inherited corpus; a second is a test that stopped running.

Requirement 6's last clause. 97 on the tree this step starts from, and the bound does not move: nothing in this milestone trades a returned value for a discard. The two places it could have -- the path variable that was read out of a map and is now read off the request, and the level that was parsed out of a string -- both still have an error or an ok to deal with, and dealing with it is the work. What the bound forbids is the ninety-seven becoming ninety-eight: shedding one is free, acquiring one is not.

Requirement 6. 84 `Test...` functions on the tree this step starts from and none of them may go. This milestone touches no test file for a reason of its own: the logging and routing layers it rewrites are exercised by the recorded corpus and by the verifier's own probe packages, neither of which lives in the tree, so a candidate who finds a test inconvenient here has no honest reason to have opened it.
Requirement 6. Ginkgo specs, counted separately from test functions because the integration suites are written in them.

Requirement 6, restated because this is the one milestone of the eight where the construct and its name come apart. `astcount` counts an assertion as a call to `Expect`, `Expectf` or the ginkgo omega, a call on `assert.` or `require.`, or a call to `Error`, `Errorf`, `Fatal` or `Fatalf` on a receiver that is not a bare identifier. The last clause is there to catch `t.Errorf` reached through a struct field or a renamed closure argument, and it catches a logging call on a method chain just as readily: 36 of the 503 on the tree this step starts from are log statements in non-test files, `ctx.WithFields(lf).Error(...)` and its relatives. Requirement 3 retires eight of those 36 -- the four calls on the logrus `*log.Logger` and the four on the `*log.Entry` the entry wrapper embeds, all in `api/context/context_logger.go`, all of which cease to exist when the types they are called on do. The other 28 survive unchanged, because a chain onto the ported `types.FieldLogger` is still a call on a non-identifier receiver. The reference tree therefore lands at 495 with no test file opened, and the bound is 493: eight for the calls the milestone is required to delete, and two more because `Errorf` and `Fatalf` sit on the boundary of the same judgement -- they delegate through a bare `ctx.Error` and `ctx.Fatal` here and count for nothing, and a tree that calls the structured logger directly from both counts two more without being more migrated for it. Ten counts of slack, and the slack is spendable only on what the bounds beside it do not already forbid: `floor:test-funcs` at 84, `floor:specs` at 111 and `floor:test-files` at 16 each hold their own line, so it buys no test function, no spec and no file -- it buys eight log statements the milestone names and two ways of writing the same two methods.
Requirement 6.

Requirement 6 and requirement 8's last sentence. One test file is behind a build tag today (`drivers/storage/mock/tests`); a second is a suite that stopped running under a constraint rather than in the open.

Requirement 8's last sentence, and the bound that keeps the import-graph gates honest: a file tagged out of the build vanishes from `go list -deps` just as thoroughly as a file whose import was retired. 124: step 4's floor of 125 less the one file of slack this step's own requirement 3 needs -- it rewrites the two files that declare the logging surface, `api/types/types_logger.go` at 44 lines and `api/context/context_logger.go` at 360, and folding the smaller into the type declarations beside it is a defensible shape for that answer rather than a regression. The bound is derived from what the instructions require, not from the reference's count (127), so a correct tree that added no file at steps 3 and 4 is not failed for it (wave D, 2026-10-12). Strict, for the reason step 1 recorded: proportional scoring cannot deter a single excursion against a baseline this large.

Requirement 8's last sentence, by identity rather than by count. The same twenty-one entries the previous milestones left behind, unchanged: this milestone has no reason to move any of them. Widening `//go:build darwin` or `//go:build mock` so work can be skipped, or narrowing one so it need not be done, both move this. Keys the candidate adds are not held against it, so this is a bound on loss.
Requirement 8. The `// +build` form was retired three milestones ago; a file re-acquiring one is that coming undone. Zero on both trees.

The same bound from the other side: twelve files carry a `//go:build` line and no legacy twin, on the tree this step starts from and on the finished one alike. A constraint dropped rather than kept moves this below twelve; the constraint set above says which twelve.
Requirement 7. The `golang.org/x/net/context` shim stays retired; the baseline is the four packages that reached it before it was, so the fall-off is measured on the same scale it was earned on.
Requirement 7, the same bound on the subpackage.

Requirement 7. The standard library's `context` stays live in the five first-party packages that deal in a context type. This milestone rewrites import blocks in a dozen files; a sweep that reorganised them and broke the plumbing would fail this while the two absence bounds above stayed clean.
Requirement 7. The pre-Go-1.7 twin stays gone; a file reintroduced under either name is a milestone coming undone.
Requirement 7, observed. The server's configured read and write timeouts keep taking effect at the values they are configured with.
Requirement 7, observed. Stopping the server still drains what it is serving and still closes its idle connections.

Requirement 7, observed. The drain is still bounded, so a request that never finishes still cannot keep the process alive forever. It is the half of that milestone most easily lost by accident, which is why it is carried separately here too.

Requirement 6, asked of the thing requirement 4 rewrites. The router this repository has always used and the one requirement 4 moves it to disagree about every edge of a request that is not an exact match, and they disagree quietly. Every direction below is measured against this tree rather than read off the two libraries' documentation, because the first draft of this gate had three of them backwards. A method the path does not serve is 404 with no `Allow` header here and 405 with one from `net/http.ServeMux`, and the `Allow` half is asserted on the six method-mismatch requests that ask for it and nowhere else, so the middleware's own headers on an answered request are not being priced here. A trailing slash is a plain 404 here -- `/volumes/` is not `/volumes` and is not redirected to it -- where a pattern rendered as a subtree, `/volumes/`, answers it, and the root route is the dangerous one: `/` as a `ServeMux` pattern matches everything, so a port that writes it that way turns all four unmatched paths in the second test into the root handler's 200. `%2F` is a separator here, decoded before the path is split, so `/volumes/vfs%2Fvfs-000` names one volume; `ServeMux` splits first and decodes after, so the same request names a service. A doubled separator is cleaned and redirected by both, which is why the test pins the destination rather than the fact -- `/volumes//vfs` answers 301 to `/volumes/vfs`, and a hand-rolled dispatcher that matches the raw path answers it directly instead. The traversal input is the same shape with a sharper end: `..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd` in a volume ID is decoded, cleaned, and sent 301 to `/etc/passwd`, reaching no handler in this service at all. None of those is a compile error and none of them is the route anything in the ordinary corpus asks for, which is why the seven tests drive them directly. One of the seven is the thing the standard router cannot do at all: this table puts 26 routes on 21 distinct method-and-path pairs and tells the collisions apart by query string -- four handlers share `POST /volumes/{service}/{volumeID}` -- which the library being retired supports and `net/http` does not, so a faithful port has to carry that discrimination itself. A tree that drops it answers the attach handler for a detach request, or 404s a request that has an answer. Weighted at 10, above the inherited price and the second-largest weight in this family, for a measured reason: the recorded corpus does hold a scenario for this -- `routing-edges`, 27 exchanges -- and 27 exchanges of 1118 is 0.024 of the recorded score and 0.008 of the reward, which is too thin to price the whole of a routing rewrite. What 10 buys is still small and is meant to be: a regression weight scales a multiplier that lives in [0.6, 1.0], so the whole of this gate is worth 0.4 x 10/134 = 0.0299 of the reward at its very most, where a migrated weight of 10 would scale the 0.55 the body of the score is made of. The two are not commensurable and nothing here trades one against the other.

Requirement 6, asked of the thing requirement 3 rewrites, and the sharpest single defect on this rung. The library being retired numbers its levels so that a larger value is a more verbose logger; `log/slog` numbers them so that a larger value is a more severe one. `api/context/context_logger.go` holds eighteen hand-written guards of the form `if e.Logger.Level >= log.DebugLevel`, and a port that carries them across unchanged inverts every one: a build that prints debug lines when it was asked for errors only, and prints nothing when it was asked for everything. `api/types/types_context.go` declares the same ordering as seven exported constants that nothing in this tree reads, so the compiler is silent about them too. The four tests that drive one build at four settings, in both directions at each, are the whole of what says so; the inversion was produced deliberately in a copy of the tree and exactly one of these tests failed on it, which is how the targeting was checked rather than asserted. The other nine pin what the recorded corpus pins in only six lines of two expect files, and four things it does not reach at all: the rendered form is logfmt, the fields follow the message in alphabetical order, a value with a space in it is quoted and one without is not, `WithError` renders under an `error` key, and the twenty-seven-method `types.FieldLogger` surface every caller inside and outside this repository goes through is still there. The four the corpus cannot reach are the four the instruction states and nothing else here reads: a message that is empty is left out of the line rather than written as an empty field, a value that is empty is written bare rather than as two quotes, the long spelling `warning` is still a level an operator may configure and a name the parser does not know still leaves the logger at warn rather than at the standard library's own default, and the formatting and `ln` spellings on the surface above render their arguments the way the library they were written against did. Every one of them passes on the tree this step starts from, which is what makes them bounds rather than milestone gates: the first two are decisions the pinned text formatter makes (`if entry.Message != ""`, and `QuoteEmptyFields` left false), the third is a spelling its `ParseLevel` accepts beside the fall back this project's own context writes when it does not, and the last two are methods the surface gate beside this one only reads the signatures of. Weighted at 8 for the same arithmetic as the routing probe above and a thinner corpus: six lines of two CLI expect files is 0.002 of the reward, against a clause that rewrites thirty files. 0.4 x 8/134 = 0.0239 of the reward at its very most -- which is why the rendered form is also priced in the migrated family, by `probe:logging-form` over this same directory. These thirteen are bounds because all thirteen pass on the tree this step starts from; those two are a milestone gate because they do not.

Requirement 6, the controls for the package above and for the migrated gate that shares its directory, and they control three different things. The first writes a sentinel to each standard stream and reads it back, because every result above is collected by redirecting file descriptors 1 and 2 into a pipe and a collection method that has stopped working reports silence, which is indistinguishable from a logger that has stopped writing. The second asks for a line with nothing configured at all: a context with no level set still exists and an error logged on it still comes out. The third asks the same of the logger no context configured, which is the one the two migrated form checks read: a logger that writes nothing at all fails those for a reason that has nothing to do with the form it would have used, and this is what tells the two cases apart.

Requirement 5's other half, and the false friend this milestone hands a candidate. Two packages in this tree import something called `rand` and only one of them is the one requirement 5 names: `api/server/server_names.go` imports `math/rand` to pick three words out of three word lists, and `api/types/types_uuid.go` imports `crypto/rand` to fill sixteen bytes of a version-4 UUID. The AST census cannot tell them apart -- it keys selectors on the leftmost identifier, and both are `rand` -- so a gate written over the census would read `rand.Read` as evidence either way. The import graph can, and this is the gate that says the cryptographic one is still there. It is a bound rather than a milestone gate because it passes on the tree this step starts from, and it is worth 2 rather than 1 because the tree it is looking for is not a careless one: `math/rand/v2` has no `Read`, so a candidate who sweeps both imports to the new package is told by the compiler, and the tree this gate exists for is the one that answers that message by seeding a `math/rand/v2` generator and filling the UUID from it. That tree compiles, passes the corpus -- a UUID is a UUID -- and has replaced a cryptographic source with a predictable one.
